lead: Illinois water damage often starts in the basement, from storm backups to burst pipes in deep cold. DryFlare helps owners from Chicago to Springfield get water out fast.
risk: basement flooding and sewer backups, severe storms and frozen pipes
why: Much of the Chicago area has a combined sewer system. It carries both rain and sewage. Heavy rain can overload it and push sewage up through basement drains. The Deep Tunnel project helps, but storms still flood basements. In July 2023, record rain flooded thousands of homes in Chicago's West Side and Cicero.

Downstate, the Illinois and Mississippi rivers flood towns in wet years, as in 1993 and 2019. Cold snaps freeze pipes in older two-flats and bungalows. Nearly two-thirds of Illinois homes were built before 1980, so original drain lines are common. Indiana and Wisconsin see many of the same basement problems.
image_alt: Hallway with doors and trim removed during repairs
image_caption: After an Illinois basement backup, trim, doors and drywall often come out so the space can dry.
problems: Towns along the Illinois and Mississippi rivers
tips: Install a backwater valve or standpipe on basement floor drains.
Test your sump pump each spring and add a battery backup.
Keep storage boxes off the basement floor.
Check whether your city offers rebates for flood control devices.
insurance: A standard Illinois home policy does not cover sewer backup. You need to add water backup cover.

faq.q: Is a sewer backup in my Chicago basement covered by insurance?
faq.a: Only if you have water backup or sewer backup coverage, which is an add-on to most policies. Flood insurance does not cover backups unless they are caused by a general flood. Check your policy before the next storm.

licensing: Illinois has no statewide general contractor license, so Chicago and other cities license contractors locally. Plumbers and roofers need state licenses.
